samples.text:
The pie charts compare what kind of materials are in the household rubbish in two cities, City A and City B.

In City A, food waste was the largest part, it was 42% of the rubbish. Paper was 18% and plastics was 14%. Other materials was 12%, glass was 8% and textiles was the smallest with 6%. So nearly the half of rubbish in City A was food.

In City B, the situation was different. Paper was the biggest material with 29%, and food waste was only 22%, which is much more lower than City A. Plastics was 21% so it was higher than in City A too. Other was 13%, textiles was 9% and glass only 6%.

Overall, the rubbish in City A had mostly food waste, but in City B paper, plastics and food waste were more similar. Also City B had more paper and plastics than City A, and City A had more food and glass than City B.
samples.why: Accurate comparison of both charts · overview placed at the end and somewhat general · repetitive structure and linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and comparative-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The pie charts compare the composition of household rubbish in two cities, City A and City B.

Overall, food waste was by far the largest component of household rubbish in City A, whereas in City B paper was the main material and the waste was more evenly distributed between the main categories.

In City A, food waste accounted for 42% of household rubbish, more than twice the proportion of paper, which was the second largest category at 18%. Plastics made up 14%, and other materials represented 12%. Glass and textiles were the least significant, at 8% and 6% respectively.

In City B, however, paper was the largest single category, at 29%, followed by food waste at 22%, which was 20 percentage points lower than in City A. Plastics also formed a considerably larger share than in City A, at 21%. Other materials accounted for 13%, a similar figure to City A, while textiles made up 9% and glass just 6%. Therefore, City B produced proportionally more paper, plastic and textile waste than City A, but much less food waste.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main contrast · key features highlighted with accurate figures and valid comparisons · logical organisation · good range of linking devices · appropriate vocabulary with some repetition · few errors.

samples.text:
The charts compare the proportions of different materials found in household rubbish in City A and City B.

The most striking difference lies in the share of food waste, which dominated rubbish in City A but was far less prominent in City B, where paper and plastics made up a larger part of the total and the composition was more balanced overall.

In City A, food waste constituted 42% of household rubbish, almost twice the equivalent figure in City B (22%). Paper and plastics were considerably less significant, at 18% and 14% respectively, while glass (8%), textiles (6%) and other materials (12%) made up the remainder.

City B's rubbish, by contrast, was led by paper, which accounted for 29%, and plastics came a close third at 21%, one point behind food waste. Consequently, these three materials each represented roughly a fifth or more of the total, whereas in City A only food waste exceeded that level. Textiles were also somewhat more common in City B (9%), whereas glass was slightly less so (6%), and the proportion of other materials was virtually identical in the two cities, at 12% and 13%.
samples.why: Key contrasts skilfully selected · clear, well-placed overview · selective and accurate comparison of figures · sophisticated cohesion · precise vocabulary (constituted, composition) · wide range of error-free structures.
